title: Weakness and the Inability to Ambulate in a 14-Month-Old Female: A Case Report and Concise Review of Guillain-Barre Syndrome
case_prompt:
A 14-month-old girl was brought by her father because she would not walk. Twenty-four hours earlier she had been walking normally, with no history of developmental delay. In the preceding day, weakness progressed to difficulty crawling, worse on the left leg and left hand. Three weeks earlier she had pneumonia treated with cefdinir; four days earlier she received varicella, hepatitis A, and influenza vaccines. There was no history of trauma or fever; she last had a bowel movement 36 hours ago, versus daily at baseline. Family history was notable only for a maternal grandmother with multiple sclerosis.

On examination, temperature was 37.7 °C, blood pressure 88/palpable mm Hg, heart rate 150 beats/min, respirations 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. The head was atraumatic, extraocular movements intact, pupils equal and reactive. Neck was supple without lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, abdominal, and genitourinary exams were normal. Skin was without rash or bruising. Neurologically, she moved all extremities spontaneously but would not bear weight. No bony tenderness or deformity was noted. In prone position, the left lower extremity moved less than the right; in supine, she lifted the right thigh slightly but not the left when provoked. Grip strength in both hands was markedly weak. Deep tendon reflexes were absent in all extremities; head control was normal.

A basic metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, and liver‐function tests were all normal. Head CT after sedation was normal, with no fluid collections or midline shift. Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with 0 red cells, 2 white cells (100% monocytes), glucose 64 mg/dL, and protein 25 mg/dL. Gram stain showed no organisms and cultures remained negative at 3 days.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Botulism considered but excluded — “Other distinguishing features from GBS include normal reflexes, a descending paralysis, and constipation.”  
2. Transverse myelitis considered but excluded — “The common presentation is leg weakness, paralysis, back pain, urinary retention, and loss of bowel control.”  
3. Compressive myelopathy considered but excluded — “Compressive myelopathy causes destruction of spinal cord tissue due to a mass ... symptoms will include pain, numbness, paresthesia, and motor disturbances ... related to the level and degree of compression.”  
4. Poliomyelitis considered but excluded — “The symptoms are preceded by a febrile illness.”  
5. Heavy-metal poisoning considered but excluded — “Encephalopathy is almost universally present with heavy metal poisoning.”  
6. Glue sniffing considered but excluded — “The hexacarbons in glues and lacquers are neurotoxic.”  
7. Organophosphate poisoning considered but excluded — “The effects can be remembered by the common mnemonic SLUDGE, which stands for salivation, lacrimation, urination, diaphoresis, gastrointestinal motility increased, and emesis.”  
8. Tick paralysis considered but excluded — “Tick paralysis often has a history of a tick bite, or a tick is found in the hair on exam. Removal of the tick leads to resolution of symptoms.”  
9. Diphtheria considered but excluded — “Diphtheria can lead to a severe polyneuropathy secondary to demyelination but immunization status typically rules out this cause.”  
10. Porphyria considered but excluded — “Porphyria ... does occur in children but is very rare.”  
11. Myasthenia gravis considered but excluded — “Myasthenia gravis ... does not present as an acute weakness. Reflexes are preserved, and ptosis and ophthalmoplegia are almost always present.”  
12. Bilateral stroke considered but excluded — “A bilateral cerebral stroke is extremely rare but could cause bilateral paralysis and/or weakness.”  
13. Polymyositis considered but excluded — “Polymyositis causes muscle inflammation and leads to weakness of the proximal limb muscles occurring over weeks to months.”
